node-1.label: Patient developed left facial palsy with lagophthalmos and weak smile (House-Brackman V)

node-2.label: A woman in her 70s presented with impacted cerumen in the right ear, and a practice nurse performed two attempts at bilateral ear irrigation.

node-3.label: Immediately after syringing, the patient reported pain and hearing loss in the left ear, and subsequently developed purulent and blood-stained discharge in that ear.

node-4.label: ENT examination found severe otitis externa with inflammation of the external auditory canal precluding tympanic membrane view; after removal of the wick, a small anteroinferior tympanic membrane perforation was visualized.

node-5.label: Left facial palsy examination showed lagophthalmos, good static tone of the mouth, and weak movement on smiling, graded as House-Brackman V.

why.why: Expert analyses from laboratory medicine and radiology both note that CT shows left middle ear and mastoid fluid without bone erosion, audiometry confirms tympanic membrane perforation and mixed hearing loss, and the immediate post-irrigation symptoms support otitis externa with middle ear involvement. These findings strengthen the infectious/inflammatory explanation, but microbiological cultures and inflammatory markers remain unavailable, so active infection is not microbiologically confirmed. Confidence is therefore increased to 0.7.

The expert analyses support procedural trauma as a likely contributing factor, citing the immediate ipsilateral pain and discharge after bilateral ear irrigation, tympanic membrane perforation, and CT evidence of middle ear/mastoid fluid without bone erosion. Because infection with middle ear involvement may also contribute, confidence in syringing-induced facial palsy as a mechanism increases only to 0.45.

Radiology and laboratory medicine expert analyses emphasize CT evidence of left middle ear and mastoid fluid, supporting middle ear/mastoid involvement. However, the absence of bone erosion argues against coalescent mastoiditis, and the leading integrated explanation is otitis externa with middle ear involvement rather than isolated mastoiditis, so confidence is modestly increased to 0.25.

Both expert analyses state that the CT and audiometric findings strongly refute an idiopathic process and that no supportive evidence for idiopathic facial palsy has been found. The immediate temporal relationship to ear irrigation and the local infection further argue against idiopathic palsy, so confidence is reduced to 0.02.
